title: The Furuta nineteen ninety eight paper

segs.text: Section twenty two. The Furuta nineteen ninety eight paper. H pylori is a bacterium that infects the stomach, and curing it treats diseases such as peptic ulcer. Furuta and colleagues treated sixty two Japanese patients with omeprazole, a proton pump inhibitor, plus one antibiotic, amoxicillin, and compared cure rates by sip two C nineteen genotype, the enzyme that clears omeprazole.

The patients were mostly middle aged men with a gastric or duodenal ulcer. They took omeprazole twenty milligrams for eight weeks for a gastric ulcer or six weeks for a duodenal ulcer, plus amoxicillin five hundred milligrams four times a day for two weeks. In the United States, H pylori is usually treated with triple therapy, a proton pump inhibitor with two antibiotics.

The paper uses old names. The enzyme is S mephenytoin four prime hydroxylase. The normal allele is wild type, star one; the variants are m one, star two, and m two, star three. Star two and star three create a premature stop codon, so the protein is too short to work, and any two of them give no active enzyme.

Group one, two normal copies, star one star one, normal activity: cure rate twenty eight point six percent, eight of twenty eight. Group two, one normal copy and one star two or star three, some activity: sixty percent, fifteen of twenty five. Group three, two inactive copies, no activity, the poor metabolizers: all nine cured, one hundred percent. No patient was star three star three; such a patient would belong in group three.

Less enzyme means more omeprazole stays in the body. Earlier work cited by the paper gave the relative omeprazole exposure in the three groups as one, three point seven and twenty. This paper did not measure omeprazole in the blood.

The paper gives four reasons higher omeprazole levels improved cure. First, omeprazole stays high in poor metabolizers, so stomach p H stays high longer. Second, amoxicillin is unstable and less active at low p H, so a higher p H leaves more active antibiotic.

Third, omeprazole raises the amount of amoxicillin in the gastric juice, where H pylori is, and the higher p H helps it stay intact there, so the antibiotic stays in the stomach longer at levels that work. Fourth, omeprazole has some activity against H pylori of its own, presumably greater in poor metabolizers.

Ulcer healing followed the cure rates. In group three every gastric and duodenal ulcer healed, and the ulcer healed in every patient who was cured, which the authors credit to the higher cure rate and stronger acid suppression in poor metabolizers.

Does the result apply in the United States? She said, Not on the face of it. The poor metabolizer genotype is eighteen to twenty three percent in Japanese persons but three to five percent in white U S or European populations, so the group sizes differ. With genotyping, the same response is expected for the same genotype, and fewer antibiotics might be enough for the right genotypes.
